paras: The reported lynching at Marion, Arkansas, was a wire story of July 24, 1888, that a mob of white men had hanged one of the expelled Black county officials of Crittenden County at Marion the night before. A Memphis dispatch called the report unfounded the same day, and the Memphis Appeal, the governor and the county sheriff had no confirmation of it. The story nonetheless ran in papers across the country, some under headlines such as 'Reports Confirmed', and the Cleveland Gazette treated it as fact.

On July 12, according to an expelled deputy clerk, about three hundred armed white men entered the Marion courthouse, forced the colored county clerk to resign and sent the colored officials to Memphis. He said their spokesman warned them that 'your lives shall pay the penalty' if they returned.

Tension rose again on Sunday, July 22, when Dr. N. J. Stith, one of the expelled men, returned by train and was jailed under a grand jury indictment for conspiracy. A Marion special to the Atlanta Constitution said that some younger white men favored hanging him until older men insisted the law take its course, and that men had waited at the depot 'to take care of Lewis', the banished county judge, if he came.

On July 24 a 'very brief special' to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch said that one of the county's negro officials had been hanged by a mob at Marion the previous night, and one wire copy printed the town as 'Morton'. Later that day a Springfield, Missouri, dispatch quoted Townsend, a traveling auditor of the Gulf road arriving from the south, as verifying the report. In his account the victim, 'one of the banished eighteen', was seized while trying to enter the courthouse, dragged to the woods at the edge of town and hanged after a desperate struggle. Townsend gave no name and said details were hard to obtain because Marion was under armed guard, messengers were barred and the telegraph carried only train orders.

A Memphis dispatch of the same date stated that the report of a lynching at Marion was 'unfounded'. The Memphis Appeal said its reporter had found no trouble at Marion when he left on Monday afternoon, and its Little Rock correspondent wrote that a rumor naming County Judge Lewis as the victim had nothing to confirm it. Governor Hughes had received no confirmation, and Sheriff Werner of Crittenden said everything was quiet when he left Marion that morning. Neither the reporter nor the sheriff was in Marion that night, but none of the later coverage names a victim or reports a body.

No report of an inquest, arrest or confirmation of the hanging appears in the coverage. When Sheriff Werner spoke to the Appeal on July 30, he said only Stith had been arrested and that 'no white men were indicted', and he made no mention of a lynching.

Most white papers printed the two wire items under headlines that treated the hanging as settled, from the Helena Weekly Herald's 'Reports Confirmed' to the Audubon County Republican's 'White Men Lynch a Negro County Officer'. The Fort Benton River Press headed it 'One of the Negro Official Conspirators Duly Lynched', while the Savannah Morning News wrote 'Reported Hanged'. The Los Angeles Herald printed the Memphis denial beside both wire items under the heading 'Lynching Report Denied'.

The Memphis Appeal reprinted the Townsend dispatch under 'It Was Awful!' and answered it with 'The Worst Kind of Bosh', calling its source an 'idiotic romancer'. The same paper described the expulsion as 'a Rid-dance of Bad Rubbish' and printed the Little Rock Republican John McClure saying that 'they ought to have hung Lewis'.

Partisan papers used the report against the Democrats: the Arizona Journal-Miner wrote that office holding by a colored man in Arkansas was 'an offense only atoned by death'. The Cleveland Gazette, an African American weekly, accepted the story in two editorial paragraphs on July 28, placing it in 'Marion County' and describing the returning official as taken out by 'a mob of white brutes, worse than murderers'. The Gazette asked whether Black Southerners would 'ever learn to provide and prepare themselves to strike back'.

reader.title: Reported lynching at Marion, Arkansas
bases: Wire reports said a mob of white men seized and hanged a Black county official at Marion (A3, A5), though Memphis reports denied that anything happened (A5, A6).

Only an unnamed St. Louis special and a secondhand account from a railroad auditor said a mob hanged an unnamed official (A3, A5); a Memphis dispatch and the Memphis Appeal called the report unfounded, and the governor and the county sheriff had no confirmation (A5, A6), and no victim, body or inquest appears in any later report (A18).
The Post-Dispatch special and the Townsend report (A3, A5) are contradicted by a Memphis dispatch, the Memphis Appeal and the Crittenden sheriff (A5, A6).

accounts.label: Post-Dispatch special (St. Louis wire)
accounts.gist: A 'very brief special' said one of the negro county officials of Crittenden County was hanged by a mob at Marion the night before and that the race war had broken out afresh.

accounts.label: Traveling Auditor Townsend (Springfield, Mo., wire)
accounts.gist: Townsend said the victim, a county official and one of the 'banished eighteen', was seized at the courthouse, dragged to the woods and hanged; Marion was under armed guard with no messengers allowed out.

accounts.label: Memphis dispatch and Memphis Appeal
accounts.gist: The report was 'unfounded'; the Appeal's reporter found no trouble at Marion on Monday afternoon, and the governor and the sheriff had no confirmation.

accounts.label: Little Rock rumor
accounts.gist: A dispatch said to have reached Judge Blackwood reported that the whites had lynched County Judge Lewis the night before.

accounts.label: Black editorial
accounts.gist: The Cleveland Gazette accepted that one returning official 'was taken out by a mob of white brutes' and hanged.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the two wire items with headlines such as 'Reported Hanged', 'A War of Races' and 'Reports Confirmed', some calling it a 'race war' and printing the claim that whites feared 'a serious uprising of the negroes'.
The Memphis Appeal mocked the report as 'bosh' while describing the expelled officials as 'bad rubbish', and printed Judge McClure's remark that Lewis 'ought to have' been hanged.
The Fort Benton River Press headed the wire 'One of the Negro Official Conspirators Duly Lynched'.
The Arizona Journal-Miner used the report as Republican campaign material against 'Arkansaw' Democrats.
The Cleveland Gazette called it 'another dastardly outrage' by 'white brutes, worse than murderers' and urged Black Southerners to prepare to strike back.

versions.value: A Black county official was hanged by a mob at Marion on the night of July 23
The report was unfounded; Marion was quiet

conflicts.note: The confirming account is secondhand from a railroad auditor arriving in Springfield, Mo.; the denials come from Memphis, where the Appeal had a reporter at Marion on July 23, and from the sheriff and governor. Neither the reporter (gone Monday afternoon) nor the sheriff (gone Monday morning) was at Marion that night, but no later report confirms a death.
